# Regulatory memo — 21 CFR § 312.32(c)(2): deadline for notifying FDA of an unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction

**Status:** Draft for review by a qualified clinician and a regulatory affairs lead. It is not medical advice, is not for patient care, and is not a compliance determination for any specific case. All regulatory statements below are tied to the text of 21 CFR Part 312 as supplied and to the sources named in Section 2.

---

## 1. Answer

**Seven (7) calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information.**

Governing provision: **21 CFR § 312.32(c)(2)** (IND safety reporting; Subpart B of Part 312).

Verbatim, from the supplied eCFR text:

> “(2) Unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction reports. The sponsor must also notify FDA of any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction as soon as possible but in no case later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information.”

The sentence contains two distinct obligations, and only the second is a fixed number:

| Obligation | Text | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt notification | “as soon as possible” | An independent obligation that may fall **before** day 7; it is not satisfied by waiting for the outer bound |
| Outer bound | “in no case later than 7 calendar days” | Day 7 after initial receipt; a ceiling, not a target |

---

## 2. Sources and version control

| # | Source | Locator | Version / date | Retrieval and integrity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | eCFR, Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 312, § 312.32 | https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-312/subpart-B/section-312.32 | eCFR “current” as displayed at retrieval | Fetched 2026-11-23T10:39:10Z; sha256 db41c60ea129 |
| S2 | Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Volume 5, § 312.32 (print edition PDF) | https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol5/pdf/CFR-2025-title21-vol5-sec312-32.pdf | 21 CFR Ch. I, 4–1–25 edition (2025) | Fetched 2026-11-23T10:39:10Z; sha256 25450092fab4 |
| S3 | Federal Register source note carried within § 312.32 | “[75 FR 59961, Sept. 29, 2010]” | Final rule, 29 September 2010 | Quoted in S1 and S2 |

**Cross-version check.** The operative sentence in S1 and in S2 is word-for-word identical, including the figure “7 calendar days.” The 7-day figure therefore does not depend on which of the two supplied versions is treated as authoritative, and it has not changed between the 2025 print edition and the eCFR text as retrieved.

**Citation-form note.** The harness also retrieved .../subpart-D/section-312.32 and .../subpart-C/section-312.32, which returned byte-identical text. In the CFR, § 312.32 sits in **Subpart B** of Part 312; the alternate subpart paths should not be used as the citation. Cite as: *21 CFR § 312.32(c)(2)*.

---

## 3. Where the 7-day rule sits in the structure of § 312.32

| Provision | Subject | Clock and trigger |
|---|---|---|
| § 312.32(b) | Review of safety information — sponsor must promptly review all information relevant to the safety of the drug obtained or otherwise received from foreign or domestic sources, including reports from foreign regulatory authorities and foreign commercial marketing experience for drugs not marketed in the US (per S2, tail of paragraph (b)) | No fixed interval; supports the intake-and-triage process that starts the (c)(2) clock |
| § 312.32(c)(1) | IND safety reports — notify FDA **and all participating investigators** of potential serious risks, in an IND safety report | **15 calendar days** after the sponsor **determines** the information qualifies under (c)(1)(i)–(iv) |
| § 312.32(c)(1)(i) | Serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction | Category feeding (c)(1) |
| § 312.32(c)(2) | Unexpected **fatal or life-threatening** suspected adverse reaction | **7 calendar days** after the sponsor's **initial receipt** of the information; **FDA only** |
| § 312.32(c)(3) | Reporting format or frequency — FDA may require a different format/frequency, or the sponsor may propose one if the change is agreed in advance by the director of the responsible FDA review division | Mechanism by which the mechanics, not the statutory protection, may be varied |
| § 312.32(c)(4) | Investigations of marketed drugs — IND safety reports for suspected adverse reactions observed at domestic or foreign study sites; plus postmarketing safety reporting under §§ 310.305, 314.80, 600.80 | Does not displace (c)(2) |
| § 312.32(d)(2) | Follow-up information to an IND safety report — as soon as available, identified as “Followup IND Safety Report” | No fixed interval |
| § 312.32(d)(3) | Event not initially determined reportable but later shown reportable | **15 calendar days** after the determination is made |
| Closing text of § 312.32(c)(1) (per S2) | Each notification to FDA must bear prominent identification of its contents, i.e., “IND Safety Report,” and be transmitted to the responsible review division in CDER or CBER; additional data on FDA request within 15 calendar days of the request | Format requirement attaching to notifications under paragraph (c) |

**The word “also.”** Paragraph (c)(2) reads “The sponsor **must also** notify FDA…”. The 7-day notification is **additive** to, not a substitute for, the 15-day IND safety report under (c)(1). For a single fatal or life-threatening unexpected suspected adverse reaction, both obligations can attach:

- a 7-calendar-day notification to FDA, running from **initial receipt**; and
- a 15-calendar-day IND safety report to FDA **and all participating investigators**, running from the **determination** that the information qualifies under (c)(1)(i).

Filing the 15-day report does not cure a late 7-day notification, and the two clocks have different start events. This is the single most common structural misreading of the section.

---

## 4. Element-by-element reading

| Element | Where it is defined | What must be true for the (c)(2) clock to run | Effect on the clock |
|---|---|---|---|
| Suspected adverse reaction | § 312.32(a) — **definition not included in the supplied excerpt; verify** | There is evidence to suggest a causal relationship between the drug and the event (the causal-relationship standard is stated in the supplied text of (c)(1)(i)) | The sponsor's own causality adjudication is not the trigger; “initial receipt” is |
| Unexpected | § 312.32(a) — **not included in the supplied excerpt; verify** | The event is not consistent with the applicable reference safety information (investigator brochure, or the risk information in the general investigational plan/application where no brochure is required) | Expectedness is judged against the reference safety information in force at the time of the event |
| Fatal or life-threatening | § 312.32(a) — **not included in the supplied excerpt; verify** | The event resulted in death, or placed the patient at immediate risk of death from the event as it occurred | Only the fatal/life-threatening subset gets the 7-day clock; other serious and unexpected SARs get 15 days from determination |
| Sponsor | § 312.32(b)–(c) as supplied | The entity holding the IND, including information received by any of its personnel or agents | Receipt by any sponsor function or agent is receipt by the sponsor |
| Initial receipt of the information | Phrase appears in the supplied text only in (c)(2); **no separate definition supplied** | The date the sponsor first receives information sufficient to meet the three elements above | **Day 0.** Contrast (c)(1), which runs from “determines” |

**Consequence of the contrast.** Paragraph (c)(1) gives the sponsor a defined interval after its *determination*; paragraph (c)(2) deliberately does not. The 7-day clock is anchored to *receipt*, so time spent in causality assessment, expectedness review, safety-review-committee adjudication, translation, or queries back to the site does not pause or reset it. The regulation's own remedy for an incomplete picture is paragraph (d)(2) — submit relevant follow-up as soon as it is available, identified as a “Followup IND Safety Report” — not delay of the initial notification.

---

## 5. Computing the 7 calendar days

1. **Day 0** = the calendar date on which the sponsor (or a designated agent) first received the information. Any day of the week counts, including weekends and holidays.
2. **Deadline** = the 7th calendar day after day 0.
3. **No roll-forward.** Paragraph (c)(2) says “in no case later than.” The supplied text of Part 312 contains no weekend/holiday extension for this notification. A day-7 date falling on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday does not move the deadline; submit by day 7.
4. **No tolling.** Nothing in the supplied text suspends the clock for IRB review, sponsor safety-committee review, additional data gathering, site queries, or the sponsor's internal case close-out.
5. **“As soon as possible” still applies** and can require submission on day 0, 1, or 2 where the information is already complete. The 7 days is the maximum, not the plan.
6. **Document day 0 explicitly** in the case record (date, time, source, and what was received), because the whole obligation is measured from it and it is the fact most often reconstructed after the fact.

### Worked examples (calendar-day arithmetic only)

| Scenario | Day 0 (initial receipt) | Day 7 (outer bound) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mid-week receipt | Monday 3 March 2025 | Monday 10 March 2025 | 7 calendar days elapsed |
| Receipt before a weekend | Friday 7 March 2025 | Friday 14 March 2025 | The intervening weekend does not extend the deadline |
| Day 7 falls on a Sunday | Wednesday 5 March 2025 | Wednesday 12 March 2025 | If day 7 had fallen on a Sunday, submission would still be due that Sunday |
| Same-day complete information | Tuesday 1 April 2025 | Tuesday 8 April 2025 | “As soon as possible” would ordinarily require submission well before 8 April |

*These dates illustrate counting only; they are not a schedule for any real case.*

---

## 6. What “notify” covers — channel, format, and recipients

- **Recipients.** Paragraph (c)(2) requires notification to **FDA** only. Participating investigators are notified under (c)(1), which requires the sponsor to notify FDA **and all participating investigators** in the IND safety report within 15 calendar days of the determination. A sponsor that sends the 7-day notification only to investigators has not satisfied (c)(2).
- **Format.** Paragraph (c)(2) does not itself prescribe a format, but the closing text of (c)(1) (per S2) requires that “Each notification to FDA must bear prominent identification of its contents, i.e., ‘IND Safety Report,’ and must be transmitted to the review division in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research or in the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research that has responsibility for review of the IND.” Read together, the 7-day notification should be a written IND Safety Report, prominently identified and transmitted to the responsible review division. A telephone call alone, with no written report, does not satisfy that text.
- **Variance.** Under (c)(3), FDA may require a different format or frequency, and the sponsor may propose one if the change is agreed in advance by the director of the responsible review division. Any such agreement must be documented in writing before it is relied on; absent that, the (c)(2) default applies.
- **Follow-up.** Under (d)(2), relevant follow-up information must be submitted as soon as it is available and identified as a “Followup IND Safety Report.”
- **Not a causation admission.** Under (e), submission of a safety report does not necessarily reflect a conclusion by the sponsor or FDA that the drug caused or contributed to the event; the sponsor need not admit, and may deny, that the report constitutes such an admission.

---

## 7. Adjacent deadlines, for contrast (all figures in calendar days)

| Obligation | Citation | Clock starts | Interval | Recipients |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction | § 312.32(c)(2) | Sponsor's initial receipt | **7 calendar days** | FDA |
| Serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction (IND safety report) | § 312.32(c)(1), (c)(1)(i) | Sponsor determines information qualifies | 15 calendar days | FDA and all participating investigators |
| Follow-up to an IND safety report | § 312.32(d)(2) | When information is available | As soon as available (no fixed interval) | FDA, as “Followup IND Safety Report” |
| Event later determined reportable | § 312.32(d)(3) | The determination | 15 calendar days | FDA |
| Additional data on FDA request | Closing text of § 312.32(c)(1) | Receipt of FDA request | 15 calendar days | FDA |
| Investigator reporting of serious adverse events to sponsor | 21 CFR § 312.64(b) — **not in supplied excerpt; verify** | — | — | Sponsor |

---

## 8. Implementable procedure (SOP language a sponsor can adopt)

1. **Intake.** Any sponsor or agent personnel who first receives information about a possible fatal or life-threatening event records the date, time, and source of receipt in the safety database at the moment of receipt. That date is day 0.
2. **Triage within 24 hours of receipt.** Assess the three elements — suspected adverse reaction (evidence suggesting causality), unexpected (against the reference safety information in force), and fatal or life-threatening.
3. **If all three are met at intake:** open a 7-calendar-day clock (day 0 + 7), assign the case to a named safety lead, and target submission substantially before day 7 under the “as soon as possible” obligation.
4. **If one element is uncertain at intake:** do not stop the clock. Open the 7-day clock on the day-0 date, pursue the missing information in parallel, and either submit by day 7 or document, with the case record, the specific basis on which the case was determined not to meet the elements. If the case is later determined reportable, § 312.32(d)(3) sets 15 calendar days from that determination — but that provision does not retroactively excuse a missed (c)(2) clock on information the sponsor already held.
5. **Prepare the notification** as a written IND Safety Report, prominently identified as such, transmitted to the responsible review division in CDER or CBER.
6. **Second, independent clock.** Separately open the 15-calendar-day (c)(1) clock from the date of the determination, addressed to FDA **and** all participating investigators.
7. **Follow-up.** Submit relevant follow-up as soon as available, identified as “Followup IND Safety Report” (d)(2).
8. **Reconcile.** At close-out, confirm that the day-0 date in the database equals the day-0 date used for the deadline calculation, and that the 7-day notification and the 15-day IND safety report were each filed against their own start event.

---

## 9. Items to verify before this memo is finalized

These do not change the answer to the question asked (7 calendar days, from initial receipt) but must be confirmed before the memo is used operationally:

1. **Paragraph (a) definitions.** The supplied excerpt of § 312.32 covers paragraphs (b), (c), (d), and (e) only. The definitions of “adverse event,” “suspected adverse reaction,” “serious,” “unexpected,” and “life-threatening” sit in **§ 312.32(a)** and are cited above by location only; they are not quoted. Verify against § 312.32(a) before relying on the element analysis in Section 4.
2. **Investigator obligations.** 21 CFR § 312.64(b) is outside the supplied excerpt. Verify before adopting step 1 of Section 8 as a complete account of how information reaches the sponsor.
3. **Version in force on the event date.** S1 is the eCFR “current” text at retrieval 2026-11-23T10:39:10Z and S2 is the 4–1–25 print edition. For an event that occurred earlier, confirm the version in force on the relevant date; both supplied versions agree on the 7-day figure.
4. **Agency guidance.** Any FDA guidance on the format or channel of 7-day reports is outside the supplied eCFR text and is not relied on here. If the sponsor wishes to cite it, it must be obtained and cited in full.

---

## 10. Citations (full)

GovInfo PDF, retrieved 2026-11-23T10:39:10Z, sha256 25450092fab4. https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol5/pdf/CFR-2025-title21-vol5-sec312-32.pdf

4. 21 CFR § 312.32(a) (definitions) — cited by location only; text not included in the supplied excerpt.

=== 1. ANSWER ===

Under 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, as in force on 2026-11-21, the premarket notification (510(k)) submission must be made AT LEAST 90 DAYS BEFORE the person proposes to begin the introduction, or delivery for introduction, into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of the device.

Value: 90. Unit: days (calendar days).

Governing provision: 21 CFR § 807.81(a) ("When a premarket notification submission is required"), Subpart E — Premarket Notification Procedures, Part 807 (Establishment Registration and Device Listing for Manufacturers and Initial Importers of Devices), Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H, Food and Drug Administration, HHS.

=== 2. OPERATIVE TEXT, QUOTED VERBATIM ===

21 CFR § 807.81(a):

"(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:

(1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to,
(i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or
(ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.

(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.

(3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification:
(i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process.
(ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device."

Source note as printed with the section: "[42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 72 FR 73601, Dec. 28, 2007; 89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024]"

The 90-day figure sits in the single operative sentence of § 807.81(a) and is not qualified, scaled, or made device-class-dependent anywhere in Subpart E.

=== 3. VERSION CONTROL — WHY THIS IS THE TEXT IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21 ===

Three independent renderings of the same codified text were compared and agree word-for-word in the operative sentence:
- eCFR, 21 CFR § 807.81 (section view): https://ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-807/subpart-E/section-807.81 — fetched 2026-11-23T10:42:17Z, sha256 cffa5dd519c4.
- eCFR, Part 807 Subpart E (subpart view): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/part-807/subpart-E — fetched 2026-11-23T10:42:17Z, sha256 c74dcd356a8a.
- GovInfo, annual edition CFR-2025-title21-vol8, § 807.81 XML (edition date 2025-04-01): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol8/xml/CFR-2025-title21-vol8-sec807-81.xml — fetched 2026-11-23T10:42:17Z, sha256 3d969831ffaa.

Amendment history in the source note terminates at 89 FR 18792 (Mar. 15, 2024). No amendment to § 807.81 with an effective date between Mar. 15, 2024 and 2026-11-21 appears in the source note of any of the three renderings. Therefore the 90-day requirement in § 807.81(a) is the requirement in force on 2026-11-21.

Residual version risk to be closed by the reviewer before reliance (the fetches above are dated 2026-11-23, two days after the target date):
- Query the eCFR point-in-time/versioner endpoint for the target date, i.e. Title 21, part 807, subpart E as of 2026-11-21 (eCFR versioner API: /api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-21/title-21.xml?part=807&subpart=E), and confirm § 807.81(a) reads identically.
- Check the Federal Register for any document amending § 807.81 with an effective date on or before 2026-11-21 and after the last listed amendment (89 FR 18792).
If either check shows a change to the operative sentence, the 90-day value must be re-derived from the amended text; nothing else in this draft depends on the value being 90 except the worked examples in § 6.

=== 4. SCOPE — WHO AND WHAT THE 90 DAYS APPLIES TO ===

The duty attaches to "each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20" (§ 807.81(a)), and to a "device intended for human use" meeting at least one of the three criteria in (a)(1)–(a)(3): first commercial distribution of a device not substantially equivalent to a pre-1976 device or to a post-1976 device later reclassified into class I or II; first commercial distribution by a person required to register, whether or not (a)(1) applies; or a significant change/modification or major change in intended use of a device currently in or being reintroduced into commercial distribution.

Exceptions in § 807.81(b) (quoted from the same fetched text): a premarket notification is not required where "(i) A premarket approval application under section 515 of the act, or for which a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2) of the act, is pending before the Food and Drug Administration, or (ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP." § 807.81(b)(2) allows the appropriate FDA Center Director to determine that submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 satisfies the (a)(3) requirement. § 807.81(c) adds Part 1002 reporting for manufacturers of radiation-emitting electronic products.

Because the request describes the device only generically, the 90-day answer is stated for the general case; it is unaffected by device class, panel, or exemption status, because the timing clause in § 807.81(a) contains no class- or device-specific carve-out. What device-specific facts do affect is whether a submission is required at all (criteria in (a)(1)–(a)(3) versus exceptions in (b)), not how far in advance it must be made.

=== 5. WHAT THE 90 DAYS IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT ===

(a) It is a MINIMUM PRE-SUBMISSION LEAD TIME measured backwards from the proposed first commercial introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce. "At least 90 days before" sets a floor; submitting earlier satisfies the regulation.

(b) It is NOT an FDA review clock and NOT a clearance guarantee. § 807.81(a) fixes only when the submission must be made. The 90-day period does not, by its terms, obligate FDA to act within 90 days, and expiry of the 90 days does not authorise commercial distribution. The statutory gate for marketing is section 510(k) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 360(k)); the codified provisions on FDA action on a submission are in Subpart E (§ 807.100 in the current codification). NOTE FOR REVIEWER: the verbatim text of 21 U.S.C. 360(k) and of § 807.100 was not retrieved for this draft and is therefore not quoted here; it must be quoted in full from an authoritative source before this paragraph is relied on. Nothing in the 90-day figure depends on it.

(c) It is distinct from the separate 90-day period in Subpart E governing public disclosure of the existence of a premarket notification submission for a device not yet on the market, which runs "for 90 days from the date of receipt of the submission" (quoted from the fetched Subpart E page). That provision — § 807.95 (Confidentiality of information) in the current codification — is a disclosure provision, not a lead-time provision. NOTE FOR REVIEWER: the fetched excerpt of that section did not print its section number, so the § 807.95 identification must be confirmed against the eCFR page before citation. The two 90-day periods are numerically identical but legally unrelated; do not cite one for the other.

(d) Registration under § 807.20 and device listing are separate, concurrent obligations; the 90-day lead time in § 807.81(a) does not displace them, and this draft makes no statement about registration or listing deadlines because the relevant text was not retrieved.

=== 6. COUNTING CONVENTIONS AND WORKED EXAMPLES ===

Counting convention applied: 90 CALENDAR DAYS (unit: days), counted backwards from the proposed date of first commercial introduction or delivery for introduction. The regulation states "days" without a business-day qualifier; no provision in the fetched text extends the period for weekends or Federal holidays. Recommendation for the reviewer: count calendar days, and do not rely on any weekend/holiday extension.

Receipt-date convention: the regulation keys to when the person "submit[s]" the submission. Conservative and recommended practice is to count from FDA's date of receipt (the date FDA assigns the document control number), not from the courier or transmission date. Flag as an interpretation for regulatory review, not as quoted text.

Worked example 1. Proposed introduction into interstate commerce: 2027-03-01. Latest permissible submission date = 2026-12-01. Check: 2026-12-01 to 2027-03-01 = 31 days (December) + 31 days (January) + 28 days (February 2027, not a leap year) = 90 days.

Worked example 2. Proposed introduction into interstate commerce: 2027-01-04. Latest permissible submission date = 2026-10-06. Check: 2026-10-06 to 2027-01-04 = 31 days (Oct 6 -> Nov 6) + 30 days (Nov 6 -> Dec 6) = 61, + 29 days (Dec 6 -> Jan 4) = 90 days.

Caution on leap years: an interval spanning 29 February contains one extra day, so the same calendar date pair can be 91 days apart. Verify each planned date pair by direct day count rather than by subtracting three months.

=== 7. COMPANION REQUIREMENTS IN SUBPART E THAT TOUCH THE SUBMISSION (context, quoted from the fetched text) ===

§ 807.90 (Format of a premarket notification submission): "(c) Be submitted as a single version in electronic format."; "(d) Be submitted separately for each product the manufacturer intends to market."; "(e) Designated '510(k) Notification' in the cover letter." § 807.90(a)(1)–(3) route the submission to the current CDRH address posted at https://www.fda.gov/cdrhsubmissionaddress, or to CBER/CDER addresses as applicable. Source note for § 807.90 terminates at 84 FR 68339, Dec. 16, 2019.

§ 807.87 (Information required in a premarket notification submission) lists the required content, beginning "(a) The device name, including both the trade or proprietary name and the common or usual name or classification name of the device." and "(b) The establishment registration number, if applicable, of the owner or operator submitting the premarket notification submission." Source note: "[42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016]".

=== 8. UNITS AND CLINICAL-FIGURE CONSTRAINT ===

No clinical population, dose, or exposure figures arise in this question. The only numeric figure in this deliverable is the 90-day lead time, and its unit is stated: 90 days (calendar days), measured before the proposed date of introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce. No figure in this draft is compared against any threshold other than that same 90-day floor, and both worked examples were day-counted to equal exactly 90.

  Source: ICH E6(R2), §3.2.1, bullet (a).

ASK 2 — The two membership characteristics that should be included:
  (i)  At least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area — E6(R2) §3.2.1, bullet (b). Count: 1 member (minimum).
  (ii) At least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site — E6(R2) §3.2.1, bullet (c). Count: 1 member (minimum).

Arithmetic consistency: the two characteristics each carry a floor of 1 member; 1 + 1 = 2, which is ≤ the 5-member total in bullet (a), so neither characteristic implies a membership larger than the recommended minimum. E6(R2) does not require the nonscientific member and the independent member to be different individuals; a single member may satisfy both (b) and (c).

=====================================================================
2. SOURCE TEXT, VERBATIM, WITH FULL CITATION
=====================================================================

PRIMARY SOURCE
  ICH Harmonised Guideline. Integrated Addendum to ICH E6(R1): Guideline for Good Clinical Practice, E6(R2). Adopted by the Regulatory Members of the ICH Assembly under Step 4, 9 November 2016. Section 3.2 "Composition, Functions, and Operations", §3.2.1.
  Text as retrieved from the ICH database (https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E6_R2_Addendum.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23, sha256 f9518dbdf529…) and corroborated word-for-word against the FDA/HHS-hosted rendering (https://www.hhs.gov/guidance/sites/default/files/hhs-guidance-documents/FDA/E6(R2)-Good-Clinical-Practice_-Integrated-Addendum-to-ICH-E6(R1)_-_Guidance-for-Industry.pdf, fetched 2026-11-23, sha256 6e427d45ecd5…). The same document is published at EMA Step 5 as EMA/CHMP/ICH/135/1995.

VERBATIM QUOTATION — E6(R2) §3.2.1:

  "3.2 Composition, Functions, and Operations
   3.2.1 The IRB/IEC should consist of a reasonable number of members, who collectively
   have the qualifications and experience to review and evaluate the science, medical
   aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial. It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should
   include:
   (a) At least five members.
   (b) At least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area.
   (c) At least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site.
   Only those IRB/IEC members who are independent of the investigator and the sponsor
   of the trial should vote/provide opinion on a trial-related matter.
   A list of IRB/IEC members and their qualifications should be maintained."

=====================================================================
3. HOW THE ENUMERATION WAS PARSED (so the reviewer can check the reading)
=====================================================================

§3.2.1 contains one qualitative chapeau plus three lettered bullets.
  - Chapeau: "a reasonable number of members, who collectively have the qualifications and experience to review and evaluate the science, medical aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial" — qualitative; states no number.
  - Bullet (a) fixes the total: at least five members → this is the answer to Ask 1.
  - Bullets (b) and (c) are the two composition characteristics → these are the answer to Ask 2.

Therefore "the two membership characteristics" = bullets (b) and (c), because bullet (a) is the headcount and is already consumed by Ask 1. This is the only reading of §3.2.1 under which the guideline enumerates exactly two composition characteristics alongside a separate total.

Note on terminology in the answer: the guideline's own wording for (b) is "whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area" (E6(R2)). Do not silently substitute the E6(R3) phrasing "not in medical sciences" — see §6 below.

=====================================================================
4. TWO DISTINCT INDEPENDENCE REQUIREMENTS — DO NOT CONFLATE
=====================================================================

E6(R2) §3.2.1 uses "independent" twice, against different comparators:
  - Composition bullet (c): at least one member "independent of the institution/trial site" — this is a membership-composition requirement.
  - Voting sentence in the same section: "Only those IRB/IEC members who are independent of the investigator and the sponsor of the trial should vote/provide opinion on a trial-related matter" — this is an eligibility-to-vote rule, comparator = investigator and sponsor.
These are separate obligations. Satisfying (c) with one institution-independent member does not by itself establish that every voting member is independent of the investigator and sponsor, and vice versa. An SOP that collapses the two into a single attestation is a documentation gap.

=====================================================================
5. STATUS OF THE LANGUAGE: "RECOMMENDED" IS NOT ITSELF A BINDING MINIMUM
=====================================================================

- The operative verbs in §3.2.1 are "should" and "It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should include". In ICH drafting convention, "should" is advisory; "must" is not used in this section.
- Consequently, 5 members is the ICH-recommended minimum, not automatically a statutory minimum. The legally binding number for any given trial comes from the applicable national/regional regulation and the IRB/IEC's own written procedures (E6(R2) §3.2.2 and §3.3.1 require documented operating procedures and documented composition).
- Practical consequence for a sponsor or site: comply with the higher of (i) the ICH recommendation of 5 members and (ii) the applicable local requirement, and record the basis in the IRB/IEC composition documentation.

=====================================================================
6. VERSION NOTE — E6(R3) (flagged, not merged into the answer)
=====================================================================

ICH E6(R3) Guideline for Good Clinical Practice was endorsed by the Regulatory Members of the ICH Assembly under Step 4 on 06 January 2025, with an error correction dated 24 October 2025 (typographical corrections to references in Sections 1.2.5 and 3.16.4). # Regulatory correction memorandum — HUD prevalence ceiling in the legacy HDE checklist

**Prepared by:** Regulatory Affairs (Regulatory Specialist)  
**Prepared for:** Qualified clinician / regulatory reviewer — draft, not legal advice, not for patient care  
**Subject:** Replacement of the superseded 4,000-individuals-per-year figure with the ceiling in force under 21 CFR Part 814 on 2026-11-21  
**Governing instrument:** 21 CFR Part 814, Subpart H (§§814.3, 814.100, 814.102), as in force on 2026-11-21

---

## 1. Bottom line — the figure the checklist must carry

> **8,000 individuals in the United States per year, stated as an inclusive ceiling: 'not more than 8,000'.**

Exactly 8,000 **qualifies**. 8,001 does **not**. The legacy checklist's 4,000 is the pre-2016 statutory figure and is an error for current use; it must be replaced, not reconciled.

---

## 2. Controlling text (quoted verbatim)

**21 CFR §814.3(n)** — definition of *HUD*:

> '(n) **HUD** (humanitarian use device) means a medical device intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of a disease or condition that affects or is manifested in **not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year**.'

**Source / version control:** eCFR, Title 21, §814.3, URL `https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-814.3`, retrieved 2026-11-23T10:47:17Z, page digest sha256 `a92b8b1d4ba3`. The identical provision was retrieved in the Part-level fetch of `https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-814` (retrieved 2026-11-23T10:47:18Z, sha256 `7c4288803759`), which provides an internal cross-check that the subsection lettering and wording are stable across two retrieval paths.

**Corroborating provisions in the same Part (same version):**

| Provision | Operative wording (quoted) | Source digest |
|---|---|---|
| §814.100(b) | '… to encourage the discovery and use of devices intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of diseases or conditions that affect or are manifested in **not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year**.' | `9511bc8faee9` |
| §814.102(c)(3)(i) | Disapproval ground where 'there is insufficient evidence to support the estimate that the disease or condition … affects or is manifested in **not more than 8,000 people in the United States per year**' | `9511bc8faee9` |
| §814.102(c)(3)(ii) | For a diagnostic device, disapproval where '**more than 8,000 patients** in the United States would be subjected to diagnosis using the device per year' | `9511bc8faee9` |

No provision in the retrieved Part 814 text states 4,000 as a current threshold.

---

## 3. Statutory basis and documented history of the change (why the checklist is stale)

- **Statutory hook:** FD&C Act §520(m)(2), implemented by Subpart H; Subpart H source note: '61 FR 33244, June 26, 1996, unless otherwise noted' (§814.100 line, digest `9511bc8faee9`).
- **The change:** FDA's HUD Designation Program page states: 'On December 13, 2016, Section 3052 of the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. No. 114-255) changed the population estimate required to qualify for Humanitarial Use Device (HUD) designation from "fewer than 4,000" to "not more than 8,000."' (URL `https://www.fda.gov/industry/medical-products-rare-diseases-and-conditions/humanitarial-use-device-hud-designation-program`, digest `7eb8e019245a`).
- **Independent corroboration:** FDA guidance *Humanitarian Use Device (HDE) Authorizations* (download `https://www.fda.gov/media/74307/download`, digest `b77bdc99060a`), footnote 3: '21 CFR 814.3(n). As subsequently explained, the current threshold is "not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States." Before section 3052 of the Cures Act took effect, the threshold was "fewer than 4,000 individuals in the United States."'
- **Same guidance, body text:** '… the device is designed to treat or diagnose a disease or condition that affects **not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States on an annual basis**.'

**Consumption this history does not license:** the memo does **not** assume that the Cures Act change was the *last* amendation before 2026-11-21. The fetched artifacts show the text as retrived on 2026-11-23; they do not include the eCFR amendment history for §814.3. See §7 (reviewer verification).

---

## 4. How the corrected checklist must phrase the ceiling

Four attributes must survive the edit, because each one, if dropped, changes the qualifying population:

1. **Direction of the bound — inclusive.** Write **'not more than 8,000'**. Do **not** write 'fewer than 8,000' or 'under 8,000': both would wrongly exclude a condition affecting exactly 8,000. The pre-2016 text used 'fewer than' with 4,000; that phrasology must not be carried forward with the new number.
2. **Population basis — United States only.** The count is individuals **in the United States**, not global prevalence and not the number of devices sold.
3. **Time basis — per year.** The ceiling is an **annual** flow ('per year', 'on an annual basis' per FDA guidance), not a point prevalence or a lifetime cumulative count.
4. **Unit of counting — the disease or condition, with a diagnostic special case.** For a therapeutic device, count individuals affected by or manifesting the disease/condition. For a **diagnostic** device, the count is the number of patients who **would be subjected to diagnosis using the device** per year (§814.102(c)(3)(ii)); the checklist should carry that as a separate line item, because a diagnostic can face far more people than the qualifying disease cohort.

**Adjacent rule the checklist should not contradict:** if the disease/condition exceeds 8,000/year, the request may still proceed on an **'orphan subset'** — a subset limited by an inherent property of the device and/or the disease, with an explanation of why the device could not be used in all patients with the condition (FDA HUD FAQ page, digest `be4822303d15`; FDA HUD program page, digest `7eb8e019245a`; §814.102(c)(3)(iii) disaproval ground where 'the patient population defined in the request is not a medically plausible subset of a larger population'). The orphan-subset route does **not** raise the 8,000 ceiling; the ceiling on the claimed subset remains 8,000.

---

## 5. Redline instructions — propagate the correction everywhere it appears

Apply the following edits to the legacy checklist. Each row is a required change; the change note in column 4 is to be retained in the checklist's revision history.

| # | Location in checklist | Legacy text (to be removed) | Replacement text (to be inserted) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | HUD definition / eligibility criterion | '4,000 individuals per year' | '**not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year**' |
| 2 | Same line, comparison operator | 'fewer than 4,000' | '**not more than 8,000**' (inclusive) |
| 3 | Any worked example or screening quiz using 4,000 | numeric 4,000 | numeric **8,000** |
| 4 | Diagnostic-device sub-criterion (if present) | (absent, or 4,000-based) | '**not more than 8,000 patients in the United States would be subjected to diagnosis using the device per year**' (§814.102(c)(3)(ii)) |
| 5 | Citation footer | '21 CFR 814.3(n)' without version | '**21 CFR 814.3(n), as in force on 2026-11-21; ceiling = 8,000 (inclusive); superseded 4,000 (pre-Cures Act) removed**' |
| 6 | Change log | (none) | 'Revision N: HUD prevalence ceiling corrected from 4,000 to 8,000 per 21st Century Cures Act §3052 (Pub. L. 114-255, Dec 13, 2016), reflected in 21 CFR 814.3(n), 814.100(b), 814.102(c)(3)(i)–(ii).' |

**Global search strings for the editor:** `4,000`, `4000`, `fewer than`, `4 000`. Every hit must be dispositioned as either *changed* or *retired with a history note*; none may remain as a live criterion.

---

## 6. What must **not** change in this edit

- Do not alter any other numeric threshold in the checklist (review timelines, filing periods, supplement fees, IRB quorum, etc.). This memo addresses only the HUD prevalence ceiling.
- Do not replace 8,000 with any figure drawn from a **proposed** rule, a **draft** guidance, or a state/foreign rare-disease threshold. Only the codified §814.3(n) text governs.
- Do not add a 'profit' or 'comparable device' analysis to this line item; those are separate HDE eligibility criteria (§814.112(a)(2) and the HDE provision's profit prohibition) and are out of scope for this correction.

---

## 7. Currency verification the reviewer must perform before release

Residual risk stated openly: the eCFR text was retrived **2026-11-23T10:47:17Z**, i.e. **two days after** the 2026-11-21 as-of date. The memo therefore treats the retrived text as the 2026-11-21 text on the basis that no amendatory document appears in the fetched artifacts, but that is an inference, not a documented negative. Before the checklist is released:

1. On eCFR, open Title 21 §814.3 and use the **'Go to Date'** control set to **2026-11-21**; confirm subsection (n) reads 'not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year'.
2. Open the eCFR **amendment / 'Published Editions'** history for §814.3 and confirm no document effective on or before 2026-11-21 post-dates the conforming text quoted in §2 above.
3. Search the **Federal Register** for proposed and final rules affecting §814.3(n) or FD&C Act §520(m) with an effective date on or before 2026-11-21. If any exists, it displaces this memo and the checklist must be reissued against that text.
4. Confirm no relevant **court order** has vacated or enjoined the threshold as of the same date.
5. Record the verification date, the reviewer's name, and the eCFR digest in the checklist's revision log.

If step 1 or 2 produces a figure other than 8,000, **stop**: do not issue the checklist, and escalate to regulatory affairs with the eCFR permalink for the as-of-date text.

---

## 8. Summary table for the reviewer

| Item | Value | Unit | Authority (version) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HUD prevalence ceiling, current | **8,000** (inclusive) | individuals in the United States per year | 21 CFR §814.3(n), as in force 2026-11-21 |
| Same ceiling, restated in Subpart H scope provision | 8,000 | individuals in the United States per year | 21 CFR §814.100(b) |
| Diagnostic-device counting ceiling | 8,000 | patients subjected to diagnosis in the United States per year | 21 CFR §814.102(c)(3)(ii) |
| Legacy figure to be removed | 4,000 | individuals per year | Superseded by 21st Century Cures Act §3052, Pub. L. 114-255 (Dec 13, 2016) |
| First non-qualifying value | 8,001 | individuals in the United States per year | Arithmetic consequence of 'not more than 8,000' |

---

## 9. Limitations

This is a draft regulatory analysis for a qualified clinician/regulatory reviewer. It is not legal advice and is not for patient care. It is scoped to the numerical ceiling in the HUD definition and the minimum conforming edits needed to keep the checklist internally consistent; it is not a full HDE regulatory analysis and does not opine on any specific device's eligibility. The version control in §2 is limited to the artifacts actually retrived and digested above; the verification in §7 is mandatory and is not satisfied by this memo alone.

TITLE: Timing of tuberculin skin test (TST) reading and qualification of the reader — answer drawn from the CDC 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis' page as available on 2026-11-21.

=====================================================================
1. THE ANSWERS, STATED PLAINLY
=====================================================================

ASK 2 — WHEN MUST THE TST REACTION BE EXAMINED?

48–72 hours after the tuberculin is injected (i.e., after placement).

Source wording (named page, verbatim): "After 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker." (S1)

- Unit of the figure: hours, counted from the time of intradermal placement of the tuberculin dose.
- The exposure that starts the clock: 0.1 mL containing 5 tuberculin units of tuberculin PPD, injected intradermally, usually on the forearm (S4, S5).
- Population: any person on whom a Mantoux TST has been placed — the page states no restriction by age or immune status for the reading window itself. (The page separately notes CDC recommends the TB skin test as the testing method for children younger than 5 years, while noting some experts use TB blood tests in younger children — S1.)
- Lower bound is real: the reaction is not read before 48 hours. Upper bound is real: a reading after 72 hours is not accepted as the reading of that test; CDC's TST fact sheet states "A patient who does not return within 72 hours will need to be rescheduled for another skin test" and "If a person does not return within 48-72 hours for a tuberculin skin test reading, a second test can be placed as soon as possible" (S5).
- What is measured, and in what unit: the induration (firm swelling), recorded in millimetres, measured across the forearm perpendicular to the long axis; erythema (redness) is not measured (S5, S6).

ASK 3 — WHO MUST EXAMINE IT?

A trained health care worker. The patient must not read their own test.

Source wording (named page, verbatim): "...the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker. The health care worker measures any swelling where the tuberculin was injected to determine if the reaction to the test is positive or negative." (S1)

The TST-specific CDC page linked from the named page sharpens the requirement and adds the jurisdictional qualifier (verbatim): "The TB skin test should be placed (administered) and read by a designated, trained health care provider. CDC's Core Curriculum is explicit that self-reading is not acceptable (verbatim): "A trained health care worker should examine a patient's forearm 48 to 72 hours after the tuberculin is injected. Health care workers should not ask patients to read their own skin test results." (S4)

E4. Patient self-reading is prohibited; 48–72 hours restated.
  Wording: "A trained health care worker should examine a patient's forearm 48 to 72 hours after the tuberculin is injected. Health care workers should not ask patients to read their own skin test results."
  Source: S4. Unit: hours post-injection.

E5. Reading is of induration in millimetres; erythema is not measured; late readings are rescheduled.
  Wording: "The skin test reaction should be read between 48 and 72 hours after administration by a health care worker trained to read TST results. A patient who does not return within 72 hours will need to be rescheduled for another skin test. The reaction should be measured in millimeters of the induration (firm swelling). The reader should not measure erythema (redness). The diameter of the indurated area should be measured across the forearm (perpendicular to the long axis)."
  Source: S5. Unit: millimetres of induration; window in hours.

E6. Repeat testing after a missed reading.
  Wording: "If a person does not return within 48-72 hours for a tuberculin skin test reading, a second test can be placed as soon as possible. There is no contraindication to repeating the TST, unless a previous TST was associated with a severe reaction."
  Source: S5.

E7. Only a trained professional reads; training is required for proficiency.
  Wording: "The reading and interpretation of TST reactions should be conducted within 48–72 hours after administration... TST results should only be read by a trained health care professional. Training is essential for health care professionals to gain proficiency in the administration and interpretation of the TST."
  Source: S6. Unit: hours post-administration.

E8. Companion CDC page states induration explicitly, resolving S1's looser word "swelling."
  Wording: "After 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker. The health care worker measures the induration (firm swelling) where the tuberculin was injected to determine if the reaction to the test is positive or negative."
  Source: S3. Unit: millimetres (implied by 'induration'; explicit in S5).

E9. Placement parameters that define the clock's start.
  Wording: "The TST is given by using a single dose disposable tuberculin syringe to inject 0.1 ml (5 tuberculin units) of liquid tuberculin between the layers of the skin (intradermally), on the forearm... When placed correctly, the injection should produce a pale elevation of the skin (a wheal) 6 to 10 mm in diameter."
  Source: S4 (dose), S5 (wheal diameter). Units: mL, tuberculin units, mm.

=====================================================================
4. EVIDENCE APPRAISAL — WHERE IT IS SOLID AND WHERE IT IS THIN
=====================================================================

SOLID:
- The 48–72 hour window is stated identically, in hours, in all six CDC sources retrieved (S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6). No retrieved CDC source gives a different window. The equivalent lay phrasing "2-3 days" appears in S6 and is the same 48–72 hours, not a competing figure.
- That the reader must be a trained health care worker, and must not be the patient, is stated on the named page (S1) and reinforced without contradiction in S2, S4 and S6.

THIN — and the requester should be told this explicitly:
(a) CDC does not name a profession, licence, or credential. S1 says "trained health care worker"; S2 says "designated, trained health care provider"; S6 says "trained health care professional". None of these resolves whether a registered nurse, licensed practical nurse, pharmacist, medical assistant, physician, or trained community health worker may read the test. S2 explicitly delegates that determination to state and local public health authorities. Any downstream use that needs a named professional category must go to the applicable state statute/regulation or the jurisdiction's TB program — the CDC page cannot supply it.
(b) "Trained" is not defined by a curriculum, hour count, or competency assessment on any of these pages. S2 and S6 assert only that training is essential for proficiency and point to CDC's Mantoux TST Toolkit materials.
(c) What to do when the 72-hour bound is missed is NOT stated on the named page S1. The reschedule/replace rule (E5, E6) comes from the linked CDC fact sheet S5. This is an inherited, not a page-local, statement — relevant if the request is being answered strictly and only from S1.
(d) S1's own wording — "measures any swelling" — is looser than the interpretive standard. S3 and S5 make clear the measurement is induration (firm swelling) in millimetres and that erythema is not measured. A reader relying on S1 alone could mis-measure. Use S5's wording for the measurement rule.
(e) Date-of-record gap: the request specifies the page "available on 2026-11-21"; the harness retrieved it on 2026-11-23T10:50:24Z. The page displays a review date of April 17, 2025, and no intervening revision is evidenced by the retrieved content, so the quoted text is very likely identical to the 2026-11-21 state — but this is an inference, not a verified snapshot. If strict date-of-record fidelity is required, capture the Wayback Machine snapshot nearest 2026-11-21 and diff it against sha256 9095c1db7f3e.
(f) No retrieved source states an exception to the 48–72 hour window for any special population (immunocompromised, young children, pregnant people, prior BCG). The window appears to be unconditional in CDC's text. Absence of a stated exception is not evidence that none exists in clinical practice; do not convert (f) into a claim that the window is universally appropriate.

CONFLICTS FOUND: none on timing or on the requirement that a trained professional read the test. The only wording-level inconsistency is (d) above ("swelling" vs "induration"), which the more specific sources resolve.

=====================================================================
5. SCOPE BOUNDARIES — WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES NOT COVER
=====================================================================
- Interferon-gamma release assays (TB blood tests): out of scope; different specimen, different timing, different reader requirements.
- Interpretation thresholds (the 5 / 10 / 15 mm cut-points by risk group): not asked and not stated in the quoted passages; they sit in S6 Table 5 and in the ATS/IDSA/CDC 2017 diagnostic guideline, and would need separate citation.
- Two-step testing and the booster phenomenon: referenced in S5 but not part of this answer.
- Which patients should be tested at all: not part of this answer.

The health care worker measures the induration (firm swelling) at the injection site in millimetres, not erythema; a patient who does not return within 72 hours is rescheduled for another skin test [S5]. Note that CDC does not name a specific profession or credential for the reader, and that the 48–72 hour window is stated without any population-specific exception on these pages."

REGULATORY EVIDENCE SUMMARY — PMA FILING-NOTIFICATION DEADLINE UNDER 21 CFR PART 814
Operative version requested: 21 CFR Part 814 as in force on 2026-11-21. Output status: draft for review by a qualified regulatory affairs professional / clinician; not medical advice and not for patient care.

=====================================================================
1. ANSWER
=====================================================================
45 days. Under 21 CFR 814.42(a), FDA must notify the applicant whether a premarket approval application (PMA) has been filed within 45 days after FDA receives the PMA.

- Value: 45
- Unit: days (calendar days — see §4)
- Triggering event: FDA's receipt of the PMA (not the applicant's mailing date, and not the date of any subsequent correspondence)
- Nature of the act required: notification to the applicant of the filing determination — either a written filing notice (§ 814.42(b)) or a notice of refusal to file with reasons and identified deficiencies (§ 814.42(c))

=====================================================================
2. CONTROLLING TEXT, QUOTED VERBATIM, WITH FULL CITATION
=====================================================================
Authority cited: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration, Office of the Federal Register. Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR), Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H (Medical Devices), Part 814 (Premarket Approval of Medical Devices), Subpart C (Premarket Approval Application), § 814.42 "Filing a PMA." eCFR "current" text as displayed at retrieval 2026-11-23T10:53:02Z from https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/part-814/section-814.42 (retrieval digest sha256 1c98fcec130a...). Source note as published with the section: [51 FR 26364, July 22, 1986, as amended at 63 FR 5254, Feb. 2, 1998; 73 FR 49942, Aug. 25, 2008; 85 FR 18442, Apr. 2, 2020].

§ 814.42(a), verbatim:
"(a) The filing of an application means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the application is sufficiently complete to permit a substantive review. Within 45 days after a PMA is received by FDA, the agency will notify the applicant whether the application has been filed."

§ 814.42(b), verbatim (the filing-notice mechanics and the start of the review clock):
"(b) If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (e) of this section for refusing to file the PMA applies, the agency will file the PMA and will notify the applicant in writing of the filing. The notice will include the PMA reference number and the date FDA filed the PMA. The date of filing is the date that a PMA accepted for filing was received by the agency. The 180-day period for review of a PMA starts on the date of filing."

§ 814.42(c), verbatim (the refusal branch of the same notification duty):
"(c) If FDA refuses to file a PMA, the agency will notify the applicant of the reasons for the refusal. This notice will identify the deficiencies in the application that prevent filing and will include the PMA reference number."

§ 814.42(d)(2), verbatim (post-refusal procedure; note the express use of "working days"):
"(2) Request in writing within 10 working days of the date of receipt of the notice refusing to file the PMA, an informal conference with the Director of the associated Office of Health Technology to review FDA's decision not to file the PMA. FDA will hold the informal conference within 10 working days of its receipt of the request and will render its decision on filing within 5 working days after the informal conference. If, after the informal conference, FDA accepts the PMA for filing, the date of filing will be the date of the decision to accept the PMA for filing. If FDA does not reverse its decision not to file the PMA, the applicant may request reconsideration of the decision from the Director of the Office of Product Evaluation and Quality, the Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, or the Director of the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, as applicable. The Director's decision will constitute final administrative action for the purpose of judicial review."

=====================================================================
3. SCOPE: WHICH APPLICATION TYPE THE 45 DAYS APPLIES TO
=====================================================================
Population / scope of the answer: an original PMA submitted under 21 CFR Part 814, Subpart C, received by FDA. This is the population named in § 814.42(a) ("a PMA").

Explicitly out of scope of this answer, and not asserted here:
- PMA supplements under § 814.39 — not retrieved for this summary; no timeline for supplements is stated here.
- PMA amendments and resubmitted PMAs under § 814.37 — not retrieved; no timeline is stated here. Note only that § 814.42(d)(1) states that, for a resubmitted PMA accepted for filing, "the date of filing is the date FDA receives the resubmission."
- Humanitarian Device Exemptions (HDEs) under Subpart H — these are a different application type with a different filing figure: § 814.112(a) provides that "Within 30 days from the date an HDE is received by FDA, the agency will notify the applicant whether the application has been filed." The 30-day HDE figure must not be substituted for the 45-day PMA figure.

=====================================================================
4. UNITS: WHY "45 DAYS" IS READ AS CALENDAR DAYS
=====================================================================
§ 814.42(a) states "45 days" without a qualifier. Part 814 uses the qualifier "working days" expressly where it means working days — § 814.42(d)(2) uses "10 working days" twice and "5 working days" once. The unqualified "45 days" in § 814.42(a) is therefore read as calendar days.

Strength of this basis, stated honestly: it is an inference from the regulation's own usage within the same section, not a quotation from a definitions provision. I did not retrieve any Part 814 or 21 CFR Part 10 definitions section for this summary, so no definitional citation is offered. If a reviewer requires a definitional citation for "day," that is the one open verification item on units; it does not affect the number 45.

=====================================================================
5. WHAT THE 45 DAYS IS NOT — DISAMBIGUATION AGAINST ADJACENT FIGURES
=====================================================================
The following figures appear in the same regulatory neighbourhood and must not be conflated with the answer:

(a) 180 days — the substantive review period, not the filing-notification period. 21 CFR 814.40 ("Time frames for reviewing a PMA"), verbatim: "Within 180 days after receipt of an application that is accepted for filing and to which the applicant does not submit a major amendment, FDA will review the PMA and, after receiving the report and recommendation of the appropriate FDA advisory committee, send the applicant an approval order under § 814.44(d), an approvable letter under § 814.44(e), a not approvable letter under § 814.44(f), or an order denying approval under § 814.45." Source note: [51 FR 26364, July 22, 1986, as amended at 87 FR 2045, Jan. 13, 2022]; retrieved from https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/part-814/section-814.40 at 2026-11-23T10:53:03Z (sha256 fc9ad46b5ac8...). § 814.42(b) ties the two together: "The 180-day period for review of a PMA starts on the date of filing."

(b) 30 days — HDE filing notification, § 814.112(a) (see §3). Different application type.

(c) 10 working days / 5 working days — the informal-conference route after a refusal to file, § 814.42(d)(2) (see §2). These are procedural steps that follow a refusal; they are not the filing-notification deadline and they do not extend or restart the 45-day period on the face of the regulation.

(d) 7 days and 180 days — abandonment and withdrawal provisions (e.g., failure to respond to a request for additional information within 180 days; failure to communicate within 7 days of an abandonment notice). These govern abandonment, not filing notification, and are not part of the answer.

Consequence of the interaction of 45 and 180: because § 814.42(b) fixes the date of filing as the date FDA received the PMA, the 180-day review clock is backdated to receipt. The 45-day filing window therefore runs inside, and consumes part of, the 180-day review period rather than preceding it. Any scheduling plan built on these two figures must treat 180 days from receipt — not 45 + 180 — as the outer review date for a PMA accepted for filing with no major amendment.

=====================================================================
6. VERSION CONTROL FOR THE OPERATIVE DATE 2026-11-21
=====================================================================
- Text relied on: eCFR "current" snapshot retrieved 2026-11-23T10:53:02Z (sha256 1c98fcec130a...), cross-checked against the Part 814 Subpart C page retrieved 2026-11-23T10:53:03Z (sha256 966884618648...) and the Part 814 page (sha256 7c4288803759...); the § 814.42(a) sentence is identical in all three.
- Amendment history disclosed by the source note for § 814.42: last amended at 85 FR 18442, Apr. 2, 2020. No amendment to § 814.42 appears in the source note after that date, and none is listed between 2020 and the retrieval date.
- Residual verification window, disclosed rather than hidden: the snapshot is dated 2026-11-23, two days after the requested operative date of 2026-11-21. A document amendment made effective 2026-11-22 would be captured by a 2026-11-23 "current" snapshot but would not have been in force on 2026-11-21. Nothing in the source notes indicates any such amendment (the most recent listed for § 814.42 is 2020; for § 814.40, 2022). Recommended closing step before external reliance: run a point-in-time eCFR query with date = 2026-11-21 for 21 CFR 814.42 and confirm the 45-day sentence is unchanged. This is a confirmation step, not a gap in the answer.

=====================================================================
7. WHAT WAS NOT VERIFIED IN THIS SUMMARY (stated so it is not assumed)
=====================================================================
- 21 U.S.C. 360e (FD&C Act § 515) was not retrieved; no statutory text or statutory figure is quoted here, and the statutory basis for the Part 814 timeline is referenced only as the underlying authority named in the regulation itself.
- § 814.39 (PMA supplements) and § 814.37 (PMA amendments and resubmitted PMAs) were not retrieved; no timelines for those are stated.
- FDA guidance documents on PMA filing review were not retrieved; no guidance content is asserted.
- No user-fee (MDUFA) performance goal is quantified here, because no MDUFA source document was retrieved for this summary. For context only, and without a figure: user-fee performance goals are management commitments between FDA and industry and do not alter the notification deadline set by § 814.42(a); the regulation, not the performance goal, controls the legal deadline.

=====================================================================
8. HOW TO USE / HOW TO CITE
=====================================================================
Answer to be used: 45 days after FDA receives the PMA.
Citation to be used: 21 CFR 814.42(a) (eCFR, Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H, Part 814, Subpart C), as in force on 2026-11-21, with source note [51 FR 26364, July 22, 1986, as amended at 63 FR 5254, Feb. 2, 1998; 73 FR 49942, Aug. 25, 2008; 85 FR 18442, Apr. 2, 2020].
Supporting citations if the review clock is also at issue: 21 CFR 814.40 (180 days) and 21 CFR 814.42(b) (filing date = date of receipt; 180-day period starts on the date of filing).

Draft prepared for review by a qualified regulatory affairs professional or clinician. Not medical advice; not for use in patient care.
